notes:
Need to search first.I've written notes for every verse, but they're **not complete**. The research tool stopped working partway through (it hit its usage limit), so I couldn't read several sources the brief asked for: Wesley's notes (wesley.nnu.edu), anything Catholic or Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey.org, and Calvin's full page. Section 3 is mostly empty as a result. The older commentaries' chapter pages also cut off around v. 11–12, so vv. 13, 15–18 are thin.

The tradition labels in brackets (Anglican, Baptist and so on) are my own general identification of each writer, not something the pages say.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "Therefore" looks back to ch. 2. We are "holy brothers" because Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11). "Set your focus" (*katanoein*, "consider") means fixing your attention until you grasp the inner lesson. "Apostle" means something like ambassador: Jesus is the Father's final messenger. "Confession" means saying the same thing as God. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- This is the only place the Bible calls Jesus "Apostle." Ellicott quotes Bengel: as Apostle, Jesus pleads God's cause with us; as High Priest, he pleads our cause with God. The two titles probably point to Moses and Aaron. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- Our calling comes from heaven and leads to heaven. Jesus is the one our confession of faith is about. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- Gill takes the "heavenly calling" to be God's inward, effective call by grace, not just the outward preaching of the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 2**
- "Appointed" literally reads "made." Ellicott thinks it echoes 1 Samuel 12:6, where God "made" (raised up) Moses and Aaron. The comparison with Moses quotes Numbers 12:7, where the "house" is God's people Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the old Arian argument that "made" proves Christ was a created being has no basis; the word means "constituted" in an office. "In all his house" describes Moses: he was *in* the house, while Christ is *over* it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- Moses was remarkably faithful; Jesus was perfectly faithful. His past faithfulness shows he will stay faithful to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/

**v. 3**
- God glorified Moses (his shining face, his vindication against Miriam, Aaron and Korah), but glorified Jesus far more: at his baptism, transfiguration and resurrection. Guzik notes, citing Morris, that the rabbis ranked Moses above the angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- The "glory" is what Jesus received after suffering death (2:9). It probably also contrasts with the fading glory on Moses' face. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- The writer is careful not to belittle Moses. To the Jews he was the greatest man in history. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-9-endure-consider-jesus-hebrews-31-6
- *Who is the "builder"? Commentators disagree:* see v. 4.

**v. 4**
- **Christ is the builder, so Christ is God:** Gill reads "he that built all things" as Christ building the church, which proves Christ is God and far above Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm
- Steven Cole makes the same point: Jesus built God's house, so Jesus is God. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-9-endure-consider-jesus-hebrews-31-6
- **God the Father is the builder:** the Pulpit Commentary notes that the early church writers (e.g. Theodoret) read the verse as asserting Christ's deity. It sides with modern commentators instead: the Father founded the house, and Christ is the Son over it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- **Undecided:** Ellicott says the text doesn't actually call Jesus the builder, and the reasoning is hard to follow with certainty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 5**
- The Greek word for "servant" comes from the Greek Old Testament of Numbers 12:7. It means an attendant or minister rather than a slave. Moses' whole life and writings pointed ahead to what God would say "in these last days." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- "What would be spoken later" means God speaking through his Son (1:1), not later parts of Moses' Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 6**
- Moses was a servant giving witness; Christ is a Son with a natural right to rule. "Christ" appears here for the first time, signalling that what Moses pointed to has now come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- We belong to Jesus' household if we hold fast. Real commitment shows over the long run, and Philippians 1:6 promises God will finish his work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- Cole thinks "firm until the end" was probably added here by copyists from v. 14. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-9-endure-consider-jesus-hebrews-31-6
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the same possibility. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- For the "if" clause, see section 2.

**v. 7**
- Scripture is presented as what the Holy Spirit is saying now. "Today" signals urgency and a genuine invitation (Guzik, with Spurgeon). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- "Says" is present tense: what the Bible says, God is saying to us now (Cole, quoted in Precept Austin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_37-9
- Ellicott translates "if ye shall hear," not "if you are willing to hear." He discusses whether vv. 7–11 should be treated as a long quotation in brackets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 8**
- "Rebellion" and "testing" translate two Hebrew place names, Meribah and Massah. One incident came at the start of the forty years (Exodus 17) and one near the end (Numbers 20). (Pulpit and Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- Scripture sometimes says God hardens hearts. The Pulpit Commentary says there is no contradiction: hardening is God's act as judgment and man's act as his own stubbornness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- Guzik lists ways people harden their hearts: indifference, unbelief, demanding more signs, and presuming on God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/

**v. 9**
- Hebrews ties "forty years" to the people seeing God's works, whereas the Psalm ties it to God's anger. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary note that many see a parallel with the roughly forty years from Jesus' ministry to the fall of Jerusalem. They mention a Jewish tradition that the days of the Messiah last forty years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- Guzik draws the same parallel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- The "works" were God's daily care and miracles, which made their ingratitude worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 10**
- The Hebrew is very strong: "I loathed a whole generation." Despite forty years of discipline, they learned nothing of God's ways. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- Gill says God's grief is described in human terms. "Going astray in their hearts" means sins of the heart, done continually. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm
- Ray Stedman: their inner life was askew, a settled habit of complaining. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_37-9

**v. 11**
- The oath refers to Numbers 14, after the spies' report. The Greek "if they shall enter" is a Hebrew-style oath meaning a strong "never." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- "Rest" is first Canaan, but Canaan is a picture of heaven. Gill rejects the Jewish saying that the wilderness generation has no share in the world to come; many who died there, he thinks, went to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm

**v. 12**
- The Greek wording treats falling away as a real possibility for some readers, not something already happening. Unbelief is a moral fault, not just a failure to understand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- Gill calls unbelief the "mother sin." He reads "the living God" here as Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm
- Quoting Newell, Guzik says unbelief is unwillingness to trust, not inability. It is different from weak faith that is troubled by doubts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/

**v. 13**
- Encouraging each other daily requires being in fellowship. Sin deceives in what it promises, what it calls itself, and the excuses it makes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- Each sin hardens us further. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/hebrews-3.html
- Christians must care enough to get into each other's lives every day. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/be-diligent-to-enter-gods-rest

**v. 14**
- The word for "assurance" pictures someone standing firm under attack. The readers had shown this early on (10:32–34); the question was whether it would last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm (Ellicott)
- Barnes describes being joined to Christ like a branch to a vine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm
- Benson reports that John Owen read the word as our ongoing life in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm

**v. 15**
- We harden our own hearts in response to what happens to us; it isn't simply something others do to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/

**v. 16**
- All of the first generation died in the wilderness except Joshua and Caleb, despite their great privileges. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- Older readers used the King James wording, "some" provoked, instead of a question. Calvin says the writer said "some," though they were the great majority, to avoid giving offence and to hold up the believing ancestors as examples. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_hebrews/hebrews_3_14-19.htm
- Matthew Henry: although most provoked God, some believed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_003.cfm

**v. 17**
- God is grieved with those who sin and keep on sinning. In the end he deals with widespread wickedness by public judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_003.cfm
- Having refused the land, the same people went on lusting, grumbling and turning to idols. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_hebrews/hebrews_3_14-19.htm

**v. 18**
- The disobedience in v. 18 grows out of the unbelief in v. 19: unbelief came first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-3/
- Hebrews uses unbelief and disobedience interchangeably (also 4:2, 6). https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_318-19

**v. 19**
- "Unable" matters: unbelief also produced their cowardice and weakness. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-19.htm
- Benson adds that unbelief was the root of all their sins, and they were shut out even though they later wanted to enter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-19.htm
- Unbelief makes us not only unwilling but unable to receive God's blessings. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_318-19

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**vv. 6 and 14: is holding fast a condition, or a sign?**
- **Gill [Baptist, Calvinist]:** v. 6 is not a condition, and it gives no ground for anyone finally falling away. It describes who belongs to the house: true believers will keep their faith to the end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/3.htm
- On v. 14, Gill says union with Christ rests on God's eternal love, and perseverance is the evidence of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm
- **Matthew Henry [Puritan]:** believers will persevere, kept by God's power. Pressing them to persevere is one of the means Christ uses to keep them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_003.cfm
- **Calvin [Reformed]:** he praises their good start but warns that perseverance is needed, so no one relies on grace already received and grows careless. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_hebrews/hebrews_3_14-19.htm
- **Barnes [Presbyterian]:** perseverance is the only sure evidence of real faith. Early zeal that dies away shows there was never a real attachment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm
- **Pett:** the sheep may wander but Christ won't let them perish, which ensures their eternal security. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/hebrews-3.html
- **Ellicott [Anglican]:** the verse implies the readers have something they could lose. Steadfastness to the end is needed to finally receive the promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm
- **Pulpit [Anglican]:** keeping their place is conditional on faithfulness, as it was for Israel, and they could lose it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- **Meyer [German exegete]:** meeting a condition is necessary to obtain salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/3-14.htm
- **Coffman [Churches of Christ]:** perseverance is necessary to win the crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/hebrews-3.html
- I couldn't reach Wesley's own notes, so the Methodist view is missing.

**vv. 11 and 19: what is the "rest"?**
- **Heaven:** for Piper, being shut out of the rest pictures missing heaven. Readers should fear unbelief because it keeps people from salvation. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/be-diligent-to-enter-gods-rest
- **A fuller Christian life:** James Smith, quoted on Precept Austin, says unbelief also keeps God's own people from "the fullness of the blessing," a satisfied, victorious life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_318-19

## 3. Other views

- **Early church:** Athanasius, Ambrose and other Latin writers took "made" in v. 2 to mean Christ's human nature. (Reported by Ellicott and Pulpit, not read directly.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/3.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- Theodoret read v. 4 as proof of Christ's deity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hebrews/3.htm
- I found nothing on modern scholarship or on popular teachings such as prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace, so I've left those out.

**Still to do:** once the tool limit resets, it would be worth reading Calvin's full page, Wesley's notes and the Catholic, Orthodox and NET Bible sources to fill the gaps.
